# System-level experiments: summary (prefix `sys_`)

Run everything: `python -m paper.experiments.run_sys_all` (long: exps 4 and 5 start their own server/simulator on local ports with temp DBs and need an idle machine). Single: `python -m paper.experiments.sys_0N_*`. Exps 4 and 5 can re-render figures/tables from saved JSON with `--render`. This file is generated by `python -m paper.experiments.sys_summary` from `paper/results/sys_*.json`; it can be regenerated at any time without re-running the experiments.

Machine (also embedded in every `sys_*.json`; runs recorded 2026-11-11 00:44:43 to 2026-11-11 01:23:03): Intel Core i7-7700 @ 3.60GHz (4C/8T), 23.9 GB RAM, Windows-10-10.0.26300-SP0, CPython 3.11.9, numpy 2.4.6, scipy 1.17.1, matplotlib 3.11.2, cryptography 50.0.2, fastapi 0.162.3, uvicorn 0.54.0, websockets 17.2, httpx 0.28.1, scikit-learn 1.9.1, psutil 7.2.2. The laptop is the edge server. A demo server was running on the same machine during the runs.

Shared helper: `paper/experiments/sys_common.py`. All figures use `paper/experiments/style.py`. All tables are booktabs in `paper/tables/`.

## Headline numbers
- Tunnel: handshake median 26 us (p95 55 us, N=1000, in-process, 72 B on wire in 3 messages). Seal+open of a real 1.6 kB batch ~104 us (seal 38 us, open 57 us); about 13.1k msgs/s on one core (a 10 Hz device needs 10 msg/s). Overhead is exactly 36 B per message, verified on 3600 real messages. Pure AES-GCM is only ~2-4 us of that; JSON encode/decode (~24-66/16-44 us) dominates.
- Security: 18 attack classes x 1000 trials each: 100% rejected, 0 false rejects on 3000 benign messages, 0 unexpected exceptions.
- Bandwidth: normal bounded batch = 16.7 kB/s (1662 B/pkt) vs raw CAN 34.4 kB/s -> only **2.1x** reduction (5.6x vs naive per-frame JSON). Under nominal HCRL-paper DoS the reduction is 5.2x (raw 89.8 kB/s vs 17.2 kB/s). **Fuzzy is the exception: the batch is larger than the raw bus bytes** (0.43x measured, 0.57x nominal: 23.8 kB/s and 118 kB/s) because each distinct random ID adds a frame entry. Worst-case packet if all 2048 IDs appear: 112.6 kB. Observed max 12.3 kB.
- Latency: ingest-to-broadcast median 13.7 ms, p95 34.7 ms, p99 37 ms (normal, loopback, 1 device). Onset-to-alert over the full stack (10 trials each, 100% detected): dos 255, fuzzy 192, rpm_spoof 164, gear_spoof 162, steering_spoof 164 ms (medians); tunnel: replay 92, tamper 467, wrong_key 120 ms; faults: sensor_inconsistency 134 ms, overheat 10.3 s, battery_drain 17.6 s.
- Scalability: **one server process saturates at ~8 devices at 10 Hz** (12.6 ms CPU per packet, ~79 packets/s/core). N<=5: median latency 13-25 ms, p95 <68 ms. N>=10: queue grows without bound (median 8.3 s at N=10).
- Health: IsolationForest never crosses its 0.65 alert threshold on overheat or battery drain (AUROC 0.72 / 0.60), only partly on sensor inconsistency (AUROC 0.99, 9.6% of windows > 0.65); rules do the detecting. Forecaster: MAE 16.5 s (overheat) / 15.2 s (battery) over all windows, but median |err| 4.7 / 3.5 s and MAE 2.8 / 0.8 s within 5 s of the threshold; early forecasts are strongly biased high (bias +16.4 / +15.2 s).
- Cyber timeline: first alert 0.0-0.1 s after burst onset for all 4 bursts, risk >= 50 after 1.0-1.2 s, class correct 99-100% of in-burst windows, 0 non-normal windows and max risk 13 in 340 quiet windows, recovery to risk <= 20 in 3.0-5.0 s after the burst.

## Exp 1: tunnel/crypto microbenchmarks
- Files: `results/sys_microbench.json`, `tables/sys_microbench.tex`, `figures/sys_crypto_latency.{pdf,png}` (script `sys_01_microbench.py`).
- Caption draft: "Per-message latency of AES-128-GCM seal and open versus plaintext size (median line, median-to-p95 band). Open markers are real batches, which cost more than same-sized synthetic payloads because JSON encoding/decoding dominates."
- Key numbers: handshake total median 25.9 us / p95 55.4 us (server-side 12.8 us, client-side 13.1 us). Real batch medians (seal/open us): normal 37.8/57.2 (1626 B), dos 29.6/22.3 (1088 B), fuzzy 50.8/37.6 (2357 B). AES-GCM alone ~2-4 us; JSON encode 24-66 us, decode 16-44 us. Throughput seal+open: normal 13.1k msg/s, dos 18.0k msg/s, fuzzy 10.2k msg/s. Per-message overhead 36 B (observed constant for every message; WebSocket client framing adds a further 8 B at these sizes, counted separately in Exp 3).
- Method: handshake = ServerSession+ClientSession in one process, 1000 timed runs after warm-up. Seal/open timed per message with `perf_counter_ns` on 600 real batches per scenario (generated by VirtualCar at 10 Hz) and on a synthetic size sweep (64 B-32 kB, 380 timed reps per size). Throughput = back-to-back seal+open of 5000 messages. GCM-only cost measured by calling AESGCM directly.

## Exp 2: security property tests
- Files: `results/sys_security.json`, `tables/sys_security.tex` (script `sys_02_security.py`).
- Caption draft: "Tunnel security tests, 1000 independent trials per attack; all malicious inputs are rejected and all benign ones accepted."
- Key numbers: benign 3000/3000 accepted. All 18 attack cases rejected 1000/1000 (rejection exception type in brackets; full counts in the JSON): Replay: same packet, same session [ReplayError]; Replay: older packet after newer ones [ReplayError]; Replay: packet into another session [PacketCryptoError]; Replay: undelivered packet into another session [PacketCryptoError]; Ciphertext/tag bit-flip [PacketCryptoError]; Bit-flip anywhere in message [PacketCryptoError]; Header tamper: seq increased [PacketCryptoError]; Header tamper: seq rewound [PacketCryptoError]; Header tamper: device_id changed [PacketCryptoError]; Valid device 2 into device 1 session [PacketCryptoError]; Wrong PSK: handshake [HandshakeError]; Wrong key: forged DATA in live session [PacketCryptoError]; Unknown device_id: handshake [HandshakeError]; Captured HELLO replayed (new nonce) [HandshakeError]; Rogue server: forged WELCOME [HandshakeError]; Rogue server: wrong PSK [HandshakeError]; Rogue server: replayed WELCOME [HandshakeError]; Truncated DATA message [PacketCryptoError].
- Method: every case calls `common.tunnel` directly (sessions in-process, random batches from the simulator, random bit positions/seq offsets, random device ids). Rate = share of trials with the expected outcome.

## Exp 3: bandwidth
- Files: `results/sys_bandwidth.json`, `tables/sys_bandwidth.tex`, `figures/sys_bandwidth.{pdf,png}` (script `sys_03_bandwidth.py`).
- Caption draft: "Uplink bandwidth at 10 Hz for raw CAN bits, naive per-frame JSON and the bounded batch in the AES-GCM envelope, for normal traffic and each attack: (a) injection rates measured on real HCRL as in the simulator, (b) nominal HCRL-paper injection rates; (c) distribution of packet sizes."
- Key numbers (kB/s raw CAN -> bounded batch, measured/nominal): normal 34.4 -> 16.7 (2.1x); dos 10.9 -> 11.4 (0.95x) / 89.8 -> 17.2 (5.2x); fuzzy 10.4 -> 23.8 (0.43x) / 67.6 -> 118.2 (0.57x); rpm_spoof 36.5 -> 16.0 (2.3x) / 51.0 -> 16.7 (3.0x); gear 2.1x / 3.0x; steering 2.1x / 2.8x. Packet median 1662 B (normal), 11.8 kB (nominal fuzzy). Naive per-frame JSON is 94 kB/s for normal traffic, so bounded batching is 5.6x smaller there and 13.8x under nominal DoS.
- Method: VirtualCar (HCRL profile, fixed speed) for 30 s x 3 seeds per scenario, 100 ms windows. Raw bits = sum of `frame_bits(dlc) = int((47 + 8*dlc) * 1.2) per frame (11-bit ID, ~20% stuffing)` over all emitted frames / duration (the repo's model); naive JSON = compact JSON of every frame; bounded = real sealed packet size (`ts_ms` included). Modes: measured = simulator default: injection rate and legit-traffic crowd-out measured on real HCRL; nominal = HCRL-paper nominal injection rates (dos 3333/s, fuzzy 2000/s, spoof 1000/s), legit traffic kept.

## Exp 4: end-to-end latency
- Files: `results/sys_latency.json`, `tables/sys_latency.tex`, `tables/sys_ingest_latency.tex`, `figures/sys_alert_latency.{pdf,png}` (script `sys_04_latency.py`).
- Caption draft: "Attack/fault onset to alert latency through the full stack (simulator REST toggle to alert on /ws/live), 10 trials per scenario: (a) CAN and tunnel attacks, (b) faults."
- (a) Ingest-to-broadcast (own sender -> server -> /ws/live, loopback, one device, same clock): normal median 13.7 ms / p95 34.7 / p99 37 (n=380, 0.0% > 100 ms); dos 13.6/36.2/38.4; fuzzy 13.8/35.4/37.4. Per-stage in-process medians for a normal batch: decrypt 0.07 ms, decode 0.06 ms, **analytics 11.7 ms**, JSON serialisation 0.08 ms (analytics is ~98% of server compute; the IsolationForest `score_samples` call dominates; 4.4 ms under fuzzy where the health vector is unavailable).
- (b) Onset-to-alert (median / p95, 10/10 detected each): dos 255/289, fuzzy 192/273, rpm_spoof 164/197, gear_spoof 162/194, steering_spoof 164/182, replay 92/172, tamper 467/473, wrong_key 120/159, sensor_inconsistency 134/161 ms; overheat 10.3 s / 10.4 s; battery_drain 17.6 s / 17.7 s. Time until `attack_class` leaves normal equals the alert time for CAN attacks (medians within 1.2 ms) and is later for tunnel events (replay 157 ms, tamper 547 ms). Tamper is slow (467 ms vs replay 92 ms) because the simulator tampers only a subset of packets, so the first tampered packet arrives later. For overheat and battery the first alert is the threshold alert; the forecast alert did not come earlier in these runs.
- Method: real `server.app.main` and `simulator` subprocesses (local ports, temp DB). (a) sender is a `ClientSession` on a real WebSocket, packets matched to broadcasts by the per-device `packets_ok` counter, both timestamps from `perf_counter_ns` in one process. (b) an async `/ws/live` client records alerts; onset = time just before the REST POST (includes the REST round trip, median 5.6 ms, max 8.7 ms); each trial waits for health >= 85 and risk <= 20 plus the per-category alert cooldown before toggling.

## Exp 5: server scalability
- Files: `results/sys_scalability.json`, `tables/sys_scalability.tex`, `figures/sys_scalability.{pdf,png}` (script `sys_05_scalability.py`).
- Caption draft: "Server load versus number of simulated devices streaming at 10 Hz: (a) CPU as a percentage of one core, (b) CPU time per packet, (c) ingest-to-broadcast latency (log scale, dashed line = one 100 ms window). The single-process server saturates near 8 devices."
- Key numbers (normal traffic; dos is the same within noise): N=1: 13% CPU, median 13 ms, p95 35 ms; N=2: 25% CPU, median 13 ms, p95 37 ms; N=5: 61% CPU, median 24 ms, p95 60 ms, 1.1% late; N=10: 90% CPU, median 8.3 s (queue grows); N=20/40: ~87-89% CPU, medians 18.0 s / 29.0 s. CPU per processed packet 12.2-13.1 ms for N<=10 (so capacity ~79 packets/s ~ 8 devices); RSS 153-167 MB. No packets rejected. Late (>100 ms) 0.0-1.7% up to N=5, 100% from N=10.
- Method: one server subprocess; devices 2..40 registered via POST /api/vehicles (real PSKs); N async `ClientSession` senders in one harness process at 10 Hz from pre-generated normal or dos batches, plus one /ws/live client. CPU from `psutil` process CPU time over the 30 s window (15 s for N>10). Latency matched via `packets_ok` as in Exp 4. After sending the harness waits (bounded) for the server to drain.

## Exp 6: health analytics (simulator only)
- Files: `results/sys_health.json`, figures `sys_health_timeseries`, `sys_forecast_accuracy`, `sys_anomaly_hist`; tables `sys_forecast.tex`, `sys_anomaly.tex` (script `sys_06_health.py`).
- Captions: "Signal, component health, overall health and IsolationForest score for each injected fault (shaded = fault active, dots = alerts)." / "Forecast ETA vs actual time to threshold, 60 trials per signal (30 nominal, 30 with randomised fault slope)." / "IsolationForest anomaly score distribution, normal driving vs each fault."
- Key numbers: first alerts after fault onset (fault on at 10 s, off at 42 s): overheat 10.1 s later, battery 17.5 s later (`low_battery`; `forecast_battery` at 18.6 s), sensor_inconsistency 0.1 s. Overall health drops to 53 (overheat), 53 (battery) and 72 (sensor) and is back at 100 at the end of the run. Forecaster: overheat MAE 16.5 s, median |err| 4.7 s, bias +16.4 s; battery MAE 15.2 s, median 3.5 s, bias +15.2 s. Error by remaining time (overheat): 2.8 s MAE at 0-5 s, 16.4 s MAE at 5-10 s, 43.3 s MAE at 10-20 s. First-forecast MAE is 145 s / 184 s (the fit window still contains pre-fault flat data, so the first estimates are very high). Forecast alert lead before the real threshold crossing: median 9.8 s (overheat) / 15.9 s (battery), vs 3.1 / 3.4 s for the threshold alert, i.e. the forecast gives 6.7 / 12.5 s earlier warning in 59/60 and 60/60 trials. IsolationForest: normal median 0.00, p99 0.37; overheat median 0.11 (AUROC 0.72), battery 0.05 (AUROC 0.60), sensor_inconsistency 0.48 (AUROC 0.99, 9.6% of windows above 0.65); none of the faults is detected by the IF at the 0.65 threshold in practice.
- Method: VirtualCar + VehicleAnalyzer driven in simulated time (100 ms windows, same decode path as the server); models from `server/models`. Forecast trials use random start values/seeds; half use a harness-only subclass that scales the fault slope (U(0.3,2.5)). Actual time-to-threshold from the car's noise-free true state.

## Threats to validity
1. **Simulated everything**: car, product module and "attacks" are the repo's simulator (HCRL-derived rates/payloads), not real hardware, a real CAN bus or real traffic. Attack detection times are for these generated attacks and one car profile. Health faults are linear ramps with fixed slopes and have no real labelled data.
2. **Same machine, loopback**: server, simulator and harness share one 4-core laptop, no real Wi-Fi/Internet latency, no TLS/NAT; Windows timer granularity shows up in sender jitter and the 12-13 ms minimum ingest-to-broadcast latency. A demo server was running on the same machine. The harness itself used 1-7% of a core.
3. **Onset timing** includes the REST round trip (median 5.6 ms) and the car's own tick and 100 ms batching; the alert debounce forced waits between trials, so trials are not fully independent (same car state, same seed family).
4. **Bandwidth model**: raw CAN bits use the repo's approximate `frame_bits(dlc) = int((47 + 8*dlc) * 1.2) per frame (11-bit ID, ~20% stuffing)` (no interframe space). Raw CAN rates come from the simulator's emission model (measured-HCRL mode leaves total bus traffic LOWER under DoS/fuzzy because legitimate frames are crowded out). The nominal mode exceeds the physical 500 kbps bus (dos 144% of capacity) and is an upper bound, not a feasible bus state. Bounded-batch size grows with the number of distinct IDs; it is bounded (<= ~113 kB for all 2048 IDs) but not small under fuzzing.
5. **Scalability** measures a single-process server with an ML scoring step costing 13 ms/packet; the limit (~8 devices/core) is an implementation property (sklearn per-packet call), not of the protocol. Senders are async tasks in one process; backpressure from the server throttles them at saturation, so "unprocessed at end" and the CPU-per-packet values for N=40 (normal), N=40 (dos) are affected by the drain-wait heuristic (the harness stops waiting once the server stops making progress) and are not reliable; use CPU% and the N<=10 rows. Latency at saturation is queueing delay that grows with test length, not a steady-state value.
6. **Forecast and IF evaluation** share the simulator that generated both the models' training data and the test faults (the IF was trained on `ml_training` simulator data; its poor overheat/battery sensitivity is likely because those faults stay inside its training range for most of the ramp). The forecaster is evaluated against the same linear ramps it assumes; the randomised slope condition is a harness-only modification of the stock physics.
7. **Security tests** exercise the protocol logic in-process over crafted messages; they do not cover side channels, timing attacks, PSK compromise, key rotation, DoS against the handshake, or WebSocket/TLS-layer issues. A 100% rate over 1000 trials bounds the failure probability only at roughly <0.3% (95%), and tag forgery probability is a cryptographic property of GCM that is not measured here.
8. **Microbenchmarks** are CPython on x86 with AES-NI; an ESP32 will be orders of magnitude slower per message. Results are not a firmware estimate.
9. **Sample sizes**: 10 trials per onset-latency scenario (fine for medians, weak for p95 tails), 3 seeds x 30 s for bandwidth, 60 forecast trials per signal.
